mcqs.question: You add a `PayPalProcessor` class implementing an existing `PaymentProcessor` interface, without editing `PaymentProcessor` or the existing `CreditCardProcessor` class. What does this demonstrate?
options: A Liskov Substitution Principle violation, since a new type was introduced
Nothing notable — this is how all object-oriented code is written
A dependency inversion failure, since PayPal now depends on the interface
The Open/Closed Principle in action — extension through new code, with zero modification to existing, tested code
mcqs.explanation: Adding new behavior via a new implementation of an existing interface, without touching the interface or other implementations, is the textbook OCP win: open for extension, closed for modification. It isn't an LSP concern (no substitution issue here) and depending on an interface is DIP done correctly, not a failure.

mcqs.question: In the `area(Shape shape)` method that switches on `shape.type`, what breaks down as more shape types are added?
options: Every new shape requires editing the same shared method, re-risking every branch that already worked
Java stops compiling once a switch statement has more than two cases
The method becomes unable to calculate area for existing shapes
Nothing breaks down — switch statements scale fine for any number of types
mcqs.explanation: The switch-based version violates OCP because each new shape type means editing the one shared method — every edit risks the branches that already worked. There's no Java compile limit on switch cases, and existing shapes keep computing correctly right up until someone breaks something with a new edit; the problem is the growing modification risk, not an immediate scaling failure.

mcqs.question: A pricing behavior needs to be swappable at runtime based on a config flag, without redeploying. Which extension mechanism fits better?
options: Strategy/plugin-based extension — an interchangeable interface implementation the object holds a reference to
Inheritance-based extension — subclassing the pricing class
Neither — runtime behavior swaps always require modifying the original class
A single class with an if/else branch for each pricing mode
mcqs.explanation: Strategy/plugin-based extension supports runtime swapping because the object holds a reference to an interface that can be reassigned; inheritance is fixed at compile time via subclassing and can't swap live. The if/else branch is exactly the OCP violation this compare is warning against, and runtime swaps don't inherently require modifying the original class.

mcqs.question: A team adds an abstract `ExportStrategy` interface with a single `CsvExportStrategy` implementation, with no second exporter planned or requested. What is this an example of?
options: Correct OCP application, since interfaces should always be introduced early
Speculative generality — an extension point added for a future that may never arrive, adding overhead with no present benefit
The Interface Segregation Principle, since it's a small interface
mcqs.explanation: An interface with exactly one implementation and no concrete second use case is speculative generality: it adds indirection without present benefit. OCP is best applied when variation is already happening or clearly imminent, not preemptively everywhere. This isn't an ISP or LSP scenario — there's no interface bloat or substitution issue here.
